name: Articular cartilage (chondral/osteochondral) defect of the knee
populations: people after ACL injury or patellar dislocation
summary: A focal loss of articular (hyaline) cartilage, with or without underlying bone, from impaction, shear or chronic overload. It causes activity-related pain and effusion and has very limited capacity to heal.

keyFacts.label: Prevalence
keyFacts.value: Chondral lesions in ~60% of knee arthroscopies; full-thickness defects in 36% of athletes

keyFacts.label: Healing
keyFacts.value: Hyaline cartilage is avascular and has almost no intrinsic capacity to heal

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: No accurate clinical test; MRI with cartilage-sensitive sequences or arthroscopy confirms

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI shows depth, size and subchondral bone; radiographs for loose bodies and alignment

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: 76% after cartilage surgery; ~5 months (OAT) to ~12 months (ACI)

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: 3-month active rehab trial first; 9–18 months after cartilage repair

overview:
Articular cartilage is a highly specialised, avascular and aneural hyaline tissue that distributes load and allows near-frictionless motion [r1]. Focal defects are common: chondral lesions are found in about 60% of knee arthroscopies, most often on the patella and medial femoral condyle, and usually alongside meniscal or ACL injury [r2]. Full-thickness focal defects are present in about a third of athletes' knees, and many are asymptomatic [r3].

Because cartilage has no blood supply, a defect confined to cartilage does not heal; defects that breach subchondral bone fill with mechanically inferior fibrocartilage [r1]. Management therefore aims to control symptoms and protect the joint. A structured, progressive rehabilitation program is a reasonable first step for many patients [r4,r5]. Surgery (marrow stimulation, osteochondral grafting or chondrocyte implantation) is considered for persistent symptoms, displaced fragments or larger lesions, and every surgical option requires a long, graded rehabilitation [r6,r7].

epidemiology.text: In 25,124 knee arthroscopies, chondral lesions were found in 60% of patients. Of these, 67% were focal chondral or osteochondral lesions, 29% osteoarthritis and 2% osteochondritis dissecans; 70% were accompanied by other injuries, most often a medial meniscal tear (37%) or ACL injury (36%). The patella (36%) and medial femoral condyle (34%) were the commonest sites [r2]. In another series of 31,516 arthroscopies, full-thickness (grade IV) lesions were mostly on the medial femoral condyle, and patients under 40 with grade IV lesions made up 5% of all arthroscopies [r8]. In athletes, the prevalence of full-thickness focal defects was 36%, and 14% of affected athletes were asymptomatic; medial condyle defects were twice as common as lateral (68% vs 32%) [r3].

intrinsic: ACL deficiency and recurrent giving way (repeated shear and impaction) [r2]
Meniscal deficiency or previous meniscectomy, which raise contact stress [r2,r3]
Tibiofemoral malalignment (varus or valgus) overloading one compartment
Patellar instability and maltracking (patellar and trochlear lesions)
Higher body mass and quadriceps weakness (modifiable)
extrinsic: High-impact jumping, cutting and pivoting sports [r3]
Direct blows to the flexed knee (falls, dashboard, contact)
High training loads with inadequate recovery

mechanism.summary: Acute defects occur when high compressive load is combined with shear: a landing or pivot on a flexed knee, the femorotibial impaction of an ACL pivot-shift, the shear of a patella dislocating and relocating, or a direct blow on a flexed knee. Chronic defects develop when repetitive load exceeds the capacity of cartilage in a joint with malalignment, instability or meniscal loss. The weight-bearing medial femoral condyle and the patella are most often affected [r2,r3].
sequence: The knee is flexed and loaded, for example landing from a jump on one leg.
Ground reaction force drives the femoral condyle onto the tibial plateau (axial impaction).
Rotation or translation adds shear at the cartilage surface and at the tidemark, the junction with calcified cartilage.
Impact energy kills chondrocytes and disrupts the collagen network, even if the surface looks intact.
Shear may lift a chondral flap or detach an osteochondral fragment, and subchondral bone is bruised.
A haemarthrosis (osteochondral) or slower effusion (chondral) develops; loose fragments may cause catching or locking.
Over months the rim of the defect is overloaded, so it can enlarge and the opposing surface may wear.

variants.name: With ACL rupture
variants.description: The pivot-shift impaction injures the lateral femoral condyle and posterolateral tibial plateau; chondral damage accompanies many ACL injuries [r2].

variants.name: Patellar dislocation
variants.description: Shear as the patella dislocates and relocates can fracture the medial patellar facet or lateral femoral condyle, producing osteochondral loose bodies.

variants.name: Chronic overload
variants.description: Malalignment, meniscal deficiency or instability gradually overload one compartment, causing degenerative defects that blend into early osteoarthritis.

variants.name: Direct blow
variants.description: A fall or dashboard impact on the flexed knee damages the patellar or trochlear cartilage.

anatomy.text: Hyaline articular cartilage is 2–4 mm thick on the femoral condyles and thicker on the patella. It consists of chondrocytes in an extracellular matrix of water, type II collagen and proteoglycans (mainly aggrecan) [r1]. The matrix is organised in zones: superficial collagen runs parallel to the surface to resist shear, the middle zone is oblique, and deep fibres run perpendicular and anchor through the tidemark into calcified cartilage and subchondral bone. Negatively charged proteoglycans hold water, giving cartilage its compressive stiffness and fluid-film lubrication. The tissue has no blood vessels, nerves or lymphatics; chondrocytes rely on diffusion and on cyclic loading to maintain the matrix [r1].

structures.name: Femoral condylar cartilage
structures.role: Weight-bearing surface; medial condyle is the most common site of full-thickness defects [r3,r8]

structures.name: Patellar and trochlear cartilage
structures.role: Transmits high patellofemoral compression in flexion; the patella is the most common site overall [r2]

structures.name: Tidemark and calcified cartilage
structures.role: Anchors cartilage to bone; shear concentrates here

structures.name: Subchondral bone
structures.role: Supports cartilage and absorbs load; innervated, so bone marrow lesions are painful; source of marrow cells after microfracture

structures.name: Menisci
structures.role: Share load and protect the condylar cartilage

structures.name: Quadriceps
structures.role: Absorb impact during landing; weakness increases joint loading rate

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
Cartilage fails when impact or shear exceeds the strength of the collagen network. Partial-thickness defects and full-thickness chondral defects that stop above the subchondral bone have no access to blood or marrow cells, so there is no inflammatory repair response; surviving chondrocytes cannot migrate into the defect [r1]. Injured matrix loses proteoglycan, swells and softens, and chondrocytes near the defect edge die, so the rim is overloaded and the lesion may enlarge.

When a defect breaches subchondral bone (osteochondral injury, or surgically with microfracture), marrow blood forms a clot that brings mesenchymal stem cells. These cells fill the defect with fibrocartilage rich in type I collagen. Fibrocartilage is less stiff and less durable than hyaline cartilage, which may explain the higher failure rates of marrow stimulation at long-term follow-up [r6,r7]. Concomitant meniscal deficiency, malalignment or instability must be addressed, or any repair is overloaded.

structures.name: Articular cartilage
structures.effect: Softening, fissuring, flap or full-thickness loss (ICRS grades 1–4) [r9]

structures.name: Subchondral bone
structures.effect: Bone bruise or bone marrow lesion beneath the defect; sclerosis and cyst formation in chronic lesions

structures.name: Menisci
structures.effect: Meniscal tear is the most common concomitant finding, in 37–47% of cases [r2,r3]

structures.name: ACL
structures.effect: Concomitant ACL injury in about a third of patients [r2,r3]

structures.name: Synovium
structures.effect: Cartilage debris and inflammatory mediators provoke synovitis and recurrent effusion

structures.name: Loose bodies
structures.effect: Detached chondral or osteochondral fragments can cause catching or locking

muscles.name: Quadriceps
muscles.effect: Arthrogenic muscle inhibition from effusion leads to weakness and atrophy, which reduce shock absorption and increase joint loading rate [r10]

muscles.name: Hamstrings
muscles.effect: Protective co-contraction and guarding during painful weight-bearing

muscles.name: Hip abductors and extensors
muscles.effect: Disuse weakness; poor proximal control increases dynamic knee valgus and compartment load

cellular.description: Impact kills chondrocytes by necrosis and then apoptosis near the injury site; collagen fibrils fracture and proteoglycan is lost [r1].
Inflammatory cytokines from synovium and damaged cells upregulate matrix-degrading enzymes; the matrix swells and softens.
Chondrocytes cluster but cannot fill the defect; partial and full-thickness chondral defects do not heal.
Marrow clot, mesenchymal cell differentiation and fibrocartilage fill, rich in type I collagen; matures slowly over 1–2 years.
Rim overload, opposing-surface wear and subchondral change can progress toward osteoarthritis.

systems.effect: Cartilage itself is aneural; pain comes from subchondral bone, synovium and capsule. Effusion drives quadriceps inhibition [r10].
Cartilage debris and cytokines sustain low-grade synovitis and recurrent activity-related effusion.
Patients unload the knee by reducing knee flexion in landing and shifting load to the other limb, which can perpetuate weakness.
Persistent pain, repeated surgery and long rehabilitation affect motivation and confidence; expectations need careful management.
Focal defects can enlarge and progress to osteoarthritis, particularly with meniscal deficiency or malalignment.

grading.system: ICRS (International Cartilage Regeneration & Joint Preservation Society) grade

grades.description: Superficial lesions: soft indentation and/or superficial fissures and cracks [r9].
Lesions extending to less than 50% of cartilage depth [r9].
Defects extending to more than 50% of cartilage depth, down to the calcified layer or subchondral bone plate, including blisters [r9].
grades.prognosis: Rehabilitation first; surgical repair if persistently symptomatic

grades.description: Osteochondral defect penetrating the subchondral bone [r9].
grades.prognosis: Often needs surgical management, especially if a fragment is unstable or displaced

timeframes.summary: Native cartilage does not heal, so non-operative recovery reflects settling synovitis and better muscle function over about 3 months. After cartilage repair, the repair tissue matures over 12–24 months, so rehabilitation is long and staged by procedure.

healing.description: Marrow clot fills the defect; synovitis and effusion
Mesenchymal or implanted cells proliferate and fill the defect with soft repair tissue that needs protection
Matrix production increases; repair tissue firms and integrates with the surrounding cartilage
Repair tissue continues to mature for up to 2 years

milestones.label: Full weight-bearing after MACI (accelerated protocol)
milestones.note: 6 weeks was as safe as 8 weeks in a randomised trial [r11]

timeframes.returnToSport: Depends on the procedure: about 5 months after osteochondral autograft transfer, 9 months after microfracture, 10 months after allograft and 12 months after chondrocyte implantation, with 76% returning to sport overall [r12]. Return is criteria-based and follows the surgeon's protocol.

symptoms: Activity-related, often poorly localised knee pain (condylar or anterior)
Catching, clicking or locking if a flap or loose body is present
Pain with stairs, squatting, jumping or prolonged sitting (patellofemoral lesions)
A history of acute injury with haemarthrosis, or a gradual onset in a knee with previous injury or surgery
signs: Tenderness over the femoral condyle with the knee flexed (condylar lesions)
Painful crepitus or pain under patellar compression (patellofemoral lesions)
Pain in a specific arc of loaded knee flexion, matching where the lesion contacts

subjective: Mechanism: impaction, pivot, patellar dislocation or direct blow; or gradual onset after previous knee injury or meniscectomy
Swelling: immediate haemarthrosis (osteochondral fracture) versus recurrent activity-related effusion
Mechanical symptoms: catching, locking or a sensation of a loose body
Activity and sport demands, previous surgery and rehabilitation, and patient goals
Night pain or rest pain (consider bone marrow lesion, osteonecrosis or other pathology)
Previous patellar dislocation, ACL injury or meniscectomy
observation: Gait: reduced knee flexion in loading response
palpation: Femoral condyle tenderness with the knee flexed
Effusion grading with the stroke test
rangeOfMotion: Usually full but may be painful at end range
A block to extension suggests a loose body
Note the painful arc during loaded flexion
strength: Limb symmetry index once the knee is calm
functional: Single-leg squat to identify the painful arc

specialTests.name: Stroke (sweep) test for effusion
specialTests.purpose: Detect and grade effusion, a key marker of load tolerance
specialTests.procedure: Patient supine with the knee extended. Stroke upward along the medial side of the knee to empty the medial recess, then stroke downward on the lateral side and watch the medial recess.
specialTests.positive: A wave of fluid refills the medial recess (grade trace to 3+).

specialTests.name: Patellar compression (grind) test
specialTests.procedure: With the knee extended or slightly flexed, compress the patella into the trochlea and glide it, sometimes while the patient contracts the quadriceps.
specialTests.positive: Reproduction of familiar anterior knee pain. Specificity is poor; use with imaging.

specialTests.name: Loaded painful arc (single-leg squat)
specialTests.purpose: Identify the range of flexion in which the lesion is loaded
specialTests.procedure: Observe a slow single-leg squat or step-down and note the knee angle at which pain starts and stops.
specialTests.positive: Consistent pain in a specific arc, which guides exercise ranges.

clinicalRules.name: Ottawa knee rules
clinicalRules.description: Use after acute trauma to decide on radiographs, which can show an osteochondral fragment or fracture.

outcomeMeasures.name: KOOS (Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score)
outcomeMeasures.use: Primary outcome in cartilage rehabilitation and repair studies [r5,r11]

outcomeMeasures.name: Lysholm score
outcomeMeasures.use: Commonly used in cartilage repair trials [r6]

imaging.modality: Plain radiographs (including weight-bearing and skyline views)
imaging.indication: After trauma, mechanical symptoms or persistent effusion
imaging.findings: Osteochondral fragments and loose bodies, alignment, joint-space narrowing; purely chondral defects are not visible

imaging.indication: Persistent symptoms, mechanical symptoms or haemarthrosis; to plan surgery
imaging.findings: Defect location, depth and size, subchondral bone oedema or cysts, meniscal and ligament status

imaging.indication: Reference standard for grading when surgery is planned
imaging.findings: ICRS grade, size and containment of the lesion [r9]

differentials.name: Traumatic meniscal tear
differentials.distinguishing: Joint-line tenderness and rotational provocation; MRI differentiates and the two often coexist.

differentials.name: Osteochondritis dissecans
differentials.distinguishing: Younger, often skeletally immature patient; subchondral bone lesion, classically on the lateral aspect of the medial femoral condyle.

differentials.name: Patellofemoral pain
differentials.distinguishing: Anterior knee pain without effusion or structural lesion on imaging.

differentials.name: Degenerative meniscal tear / early osteoarthritis
differentials.distinguishing: Older patient, diffuse rather than focal cartilage loss, radiographic osteoarthritis.

differentials.name: Hoffa's fat pad impingement
differentials.distinguishing: Pain below the patella either side of the patellar tendon, provoked by hyperextension.

differentials.name: Spontaneous osteonecrosis / subchondral insufficiency fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Older adult with sudden severe pain and night pain; marrow oedema with a subchondral fracture line on MRI.

redFlags: Locked knee or a palpable loose body after injury: suspect a displaced osteochondral fragment. Arrange urgent orthopaedic review, as early fixation of a fragment with bone attached is often possible.
Haemarthrosis after a patellar dislocation or pivot injury: obtain radiographs and MRI to look for an osteochondral fracture.
Hot, red, swollen knee with fever, especially after surgery or injection: suspect septic arthritis and refer for same-day assessment.
After surgery, calf pain and swelling or breathlessness: suspect DVT or PE and refer urgently.
Unremitting night pain, rest pain or systemic symptoms: investigate for osteonecrosis, insufficiency fracture, inflammatory arthritis or tumour.

management.principles: Treat the patient's symptoms and function, not the image alone; many defects are asymptomatic [r3]. Start with education, load management and a structured active rehabilitation program of cardiovascular, progressive resistance and neuromuscular training, which was feasible and produced clinically meaningful improvement over 3 months [r5,r4]. Refer for surgical opinion if symptoms persist, a fragment is loose or displaced, or the lesion is large and symptomatic. Surgery is chosen by lesion size, depth and location, the patient's age and goals, and the state of the meniscus, ligaments and alignment, which must be corrected at the same time. Advanced repair techniques give better-quality repair tissue and possibly lower long-term failure than microfracture, but outcomes are similar at 2 years [r6,r7].

medical.name: Microfracture (marrow stimulation)
medical.description: Arthroscopic perforation of the subchondral plate so marrow clot fills the defect with fibrocartilage; usually for small contained defects. Outcomes are similar to other repairs at 2 years, but long-term failure is higher than ACI [r6,r7]. Return to sport 58% at a mean of 9.1 months [r12].

medical.name: Autologous chondrocyte implantation (ACI / MACI)
medical.description: Two-stage procedure: harvested chondrocytes are cultured and implanted (on a membrane in MACI) for larger defects. Lower failure than microfracture at 10 years and more hyaline-like repair tissue [r6,r7]. Return to sport 82% at a mean of 11.8 months [r12].

medical.name: Osteochondral autograft transfer (OAT / mosaicplasty)
medical.description: Cylindrical plugs of bone and cartilage moved from a low-load area to the defect; suited to small osteochondral lesions. Highest return to sport (93%) and fastest return (5.2 months) [r12]; better results than microfracture [r7].

medical.name: Osteochondral allograft
medical.description: Donor bone–cartilage graft for large or deep osteochondral defects and revision surgery; return to sport 88% [r12].

medical.name: Fixation of an acute osteochondral fragment
medical.description: Early reattachment of a displaced fragment with bone attached (e.g. after patellar dislocation) preserves native hyaline cartilage.

medical.name: Correction of malalignment, instability or meniscal deficiency
medical.description: Osteotomy, ACL reconstruction or meniscal surgery alongside cartilage repair so the repair is not overloaded.

medical.name: Mesenchymal stem cell injections
medical.description: Clinical evidence is preliminary and low quality, without randomised trials; use only within research [r13].

physio.name: Structured active rehabilitation (first line)
physio.description: About 3 months of cardiovascular training, progressive knee and hip resistance training and neuromuscular training, progressed by pain and effusion. In a feasibility study, adherence was 83%, adverse events were 9% and function improved meaningfully [r5,r4].

physio.name: Graded post-operative weight-bearing
physio.description: Protect the repair with partial weight-bearing, then progress. After femoral condyle MACI, full weight-bearing by 6 weeks was as safe as 8 weeks, with earlier recovery of extension and better quality of life [r11,r14].

physio.name: Lesion-specific range and load protection
physio.description: Condylar repairs need weight-bearing protection but early free ROM. Patellofemoral repairs usually allow weight-bearing in extension but limit loaded flexion so the repair is not compressed.

physio.name: Quadriceps strengthening and AMI management
physio.description: Effusion control, cryotherapy and NMES to counter inhibition, then progressive strengthening in pain-free arcs [r10].

physio.name: Load management and education
physio.description: Explain that cartilage has limited healing, that pain and effusion guide loading, and that strength protects the joint. Modify high-impact load temporarily.

physio.name: Early return to impact or pivoting sport after repair
physio.description: Returning before the repair tissue has matured and strength criteria are met risks graft failure.

education: Cartilage has no blood supply, so it does not heal like skin or bone. Strong muscles and well-judged loading help the knee cope.
Many people have cartilage defects on scans without pain. The goal is a knee that tolerates your activities.
Swelling the day after exercise is a sign the load was too much; reduce it and build up again.
If surgery is needed, recovery takes 6–12 months or more because the repair tissue matures slowly.
Keeping a healthy body weight and staying strong are the best long-term protection for your joint.

rehab.overview: Use the same criteria-based stages for rehabilitation-first care and after surgery, adjusting timeframes and precautions to the procedure and lesion site. The non-operative program combines cardiovascular, progressive resistance and neuromuscular training over about 3 months [r5]. After cartilage repair, the surgeon's protocol sets weight-bearing and range limits; timeframes in brackets are typical after microfracture or MACI. Progress when effusion stays at trace or less and pain settles within 24 hours [r4].

stages.name: Protect & restore motion
precautions: After condylar repair: partial weight-bearing as prescribed; full weight-bearing after MACI typically by 6–8 weeks [r11,r14]
After patellofemoral repair: weight-bearing in a brace locked in extension; limit loaded flexion

exercises.name: Stationary bike, no resistance
exercises.dosage: 10–15 min daily once 100–110° flexion is available

progressionCriteria: Weight-bearing status permitted by the surgeon (post-operative)

stages.name: Progressive loading
goals: Build quadriceps and hip strength in pain-free arcs
precautions: Keep closed-chain exercises out of the arc in which the lesion is loaded
Increase load by no more than about 10–20% per week; monitor next-day effusion

exercises.name: Mini squat in a pain-free range
Seated knee extension (protected arc)
exercises.cues: For patellofemoral lesions use 90–45°; for condylar lesions avoid end-range compression early

stages.name: Strength & neuromuscular control
goals: Good single-leg squat and landing mechanics
precautions: No running until strength and effusion criteria are met
progressionCriteria: Single-leg squat to 60° with good alignment

stages.name: Running, impact & return to sport
precautions: After repair, follow the surgeon's minimum time before impact and pivoting (commonly 6–9 months after microfracture or ACI)
Monitor effusion closely when impact is introduced

exercises.name: Walk–run progression
exercises.dosage: Alternate days, increasing running time by 10–20% per week

criteria: Hop test LSI ≥90% with good landing mechanics
Minimum time after repair met and surgeon clearance (≈5 months after OAT to ≈12 months after ACI) [r12]
tests: Single, triple and crossover hop tests

prognosis: Many focal defects are asymptomatic and remain so [r3]. With rehabilitation alone, clinically meaningful improvement in function and strength is possible over 3 months [r5]. After surgery, 76% of athletes return to sport, with rates from 58% after microfracture to 93% after osteochondral autograft transfer [r12]. Outcomes of the main repair procedures are similar at 2 years, but microfracture has higher failure at 10 years than ACI [r6,r7]. Older age and larger defects are associated with poorer repair tissue on MRI [r14]. Untreated lesions in knees with meniscal deficiency, instability or malalignment may progress toward osteoarthritis.
prevention: Prompt management of ACL injury and patellar instability to limit repeated impaction and shear.
Preserve the meniscus where possible (repair rather than resection).
Maintain quadriceps strength and landing technique in jumping and pivoting sports.
clinicalPearls: A defect on MRI is not necessarily the pain generator; over one in ten athletes with full-thickness defects have no symptoms [r3].
Effusion is your best load monitor. If the knee is more swollen the next morning, the previous session was too much.
Find the painful arc and train around it; condylar and patellofemoral lesions are loaded at different knee angles.
A haemarthrosis after a patellar dislocation needs imaging for an osteochondral fragment; fixation is time-sensitive.
Ask what else is wrong with the knee. Meniscal deficiency, instability or malalignment will defeat any cartilage repair if left unaddressed.

animation.title: How a knee cartilage defect happens

captions.text: A basketball player jumps for a rebound.
She lands mostly on the right leg, which is only slightly bent.
The femoral condyle is driven onto the tibia while the knee twists.
Impact and shear damage the cartilage surface and the bone beneath it.
Pain is vague at first; the knee swells after activity over the following weeks.
Zooming into the right knee, viewed from the front with the patella reflected.

actions.text: Hyaline cartilage: no blood vessels or nerves

captions.text: The femoral condyles are covered by smooth hyaline cartilage with no blood supply.
On landing, the medial condyle is driven into the tibia with a twisting shear.
Cartilage cells die and the surface splits; the bone beneath is bruised.
Over weeks the damaged area is shed, leaving a defect down to the calcified layer.
Debris inflames the synovium: activity-related swelling is the hallmark.
The defect rim is overloaded, so without good load management it can slowly enlarge.
Healthy cartilage: sparse chondrocytes in a matrix of type II collagen and water-binding proteoglycan.
Impact fractures collagen fibrils and squeezes out water.
Chondrocytes near the impact die and cannot be replaced from a blood supply.
Proteoglycan is lost, the matrix softens and the surface breaks down.
Only if the bone is breached do marrow cells arrive; they make weaker fibrocartilage.
Overloaded edges and the opposing surface can degenerate toward osteoarthritis.
